title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a concise nearest‑work comparison, and precise preregistered protocol modifications required to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, no transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two contrasting architectural approaches are common in recent research and engineering practice. Translation‑first architectures constrain the generation space via a vendor‑aware DSL, apply formal verification, and rely on solver/repair only when constraints are violated; these approaches prioritize deterministic device guarantees. Agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines centralize generation in a single LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repair/rollback to achieve correctness while preserving generator flexibility.

This study's preregistered head‑to‑head question was: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), and analysis by the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Key design choice and its consequence. Crucially, the preregistration and execution adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics: each paired task used a single LLM candidate generated once and provided identically to both downstream architectures. This choice deliberately removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and therefore turns the experiment into a validator‑acceptance parity test for identical candidates rather than an independent generator or repair efficacy comparison. We report the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts that support an unambiguous interpretation of the observed outcomes and of what the run does and does not test.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions frame our contribution. First, formal translation→verification work demonstrates how constrained translation plus deterministic verification yields strong device guarantees and supports what‑if analyses and incremental checks; representative foundational works include network verification and synthesis systems that emphasize soundness and tractable analyses [10,11,12]. Second, LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research examines flexible generation, chain‑of‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair; these studies emphasize the need for deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [3,4,5].

Nearest‑work comparison matrix (compact). We position the present run relative to three representative verified studies along four experimental axes (independent generation sampling, repair loop instrumentation, validator acceptance focus, emulator/hardware realism):
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: evaluated independent generation sampling by LLM agents and translation pipelines (independent generation: yes; repair loops: limited; validator acceptance: partial; emulator: yes).
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: self‑correcting multi‑agent verifier pipeline with active repair/verification loops (independent generation: yes; repair loops: yes; validator acceptance: emphasized; emulator/hardware: Kubernetes policy domain).
• Weighted NetKAT / formal verification literature [5,10–12]: formal guarantees and solver‑based synthesis (independent generation: not applicable; repair loops: solver‑based; validator acceptance: core; emulator: verification models).

The present run differs from those prior works by combining preregistration, an archived paired design, and deterministic per‑task validator traces under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the result precisely measures validator acceptance parity for identical candidates but does not exercise independent sampling or repair coverage. The compact matrix above and full citations in the references situate these distinctions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory estimand. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and allowed repair_iterations = 1. The preregistration also specified shared_initial_candidate generation semantics and the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar test). The preregistration artifact is archived and its SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract. The execution adapter implemented shared_initial_candidate: the orchestration made a single LLM generation per task pair and supplied the identical text candidate to both the translation‑first and agentic orchestration arms. Practical consequences are visible in the execution manifest: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). The provider audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, demonstrating execution isolation and adherence to the preregistered contamination controls.

Task generation, validator rules, and scoring mechanics. Tasks were produced by a deterministic synthetic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest entry contains the intent, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, difficulty metadata, and a canonical reference answer (examples in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative artifacts such as task‑000001 entries). The validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5 v5.0) applies a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and a boolean validation_after.valid. A configuration passes the end‑to‑end correctness check only if validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags; these files serve as the canonical evidence of per‑task decisions. Representative per‑task validator traces (for example execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Analysis executor and statistical specifics. Analysis followed paired_binary_analysis_v1 as preregistered. The primary analysis computed paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference (A − B), a bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes. The analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap parameters recorded), and deterministic_reconciliation.json. Secondary estimands (repair coverage and repair iterations) and multiplicity rules (Benjamini–Hochberg for subgroup tests) were preregistered; secondary analysis is reported when applicable.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (single shared generation per pair), and artifact_hash_summary with the full manifest reference. Deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit counts consistent with the single shared generation stage.

Primary numeric outcomes. Deterministic scoring produced the paired contingency recorded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv: n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The primary estimand (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl lists bootstrap_resamples = 10000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729. Exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. All analysis outputs are archived at analysis/results.json and supporting CSVs.

Repair and secondary outcomes. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied = false). Consequently preregistered secondary estimands concerning repair coverage (H2) are unobserved in this execution. Representative per‑task traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) show shared_initial_candidate and validation_after.valid = true, with repair_applied = false.

Contamination and missingness checks. The preregistered contamination checks produced no flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 120 with no observed failures. Provider audit metadata indicates cache_miss_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation and adherence to the preregistered contamination_plan.

Representative example. For pair‑000001 the shared candidate equals the canonical reference modulo ordering normalization; execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json documents normalized_response, validator normalization, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and validation_after.valid = true. Similar representative artifacts for additional pairs (task‑000002, task‑000003, ...) are archived and referenced in the execution manifest and in execution/scoring examples.
sections.discussion:
What was measured — and what was not. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were used, the present experiment isolates validator‑acceptance parity: given identical LLM candidates, do downstream translation‑first and agentic orchestration paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The observed degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) answers this restricted question: both validators accepted the identical candidates for every paired task. The run does not, by design, exercise independent generator variance, sampling effects, or repair efficacy; therefore claims about which architecture would produce more correct initial candidates when operating independently are untested.

Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (compact). We map preregistered hypotheses and estimands to executed measurements and archived artifacts:
1) H1 (Paired difference A − B in end‑to‑end correctness): Measured estimand in this execution = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Supporting artifacts: preregistration (preregistration_sha256 recorded in execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0). Verdict: Tested only for validator‑acceptance parity; independent generator comparison remains untested.
2) H2 (Agentic pipeline higher repair coverage): Measured? No — repair_applied = false for all episodes. Supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied=false per episode), analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Verdict: Unobserved in this execution.
3) Secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations): Unobserved because repair_applied counts are zero; artifacts include scoring JSONs and analysis CSVs listed above.

Operational implications and protocol recommendations. The artifact bundle documents a reproducible protocol for validator regression testing and for measuring acceptance‑parity when generation is held constant; this is useful for validator regression and orchestrator equivalence checks. To discriminate architectures on independent generator and repair performance the preregistered protocol must be modified (all modifications are preregisterable and manifestable): (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm obtains an independent LLM generation per pair — model_calls_used would increase to 240 for initial candidates alone (preregistration and execution contract anticipate this change); (ii) allow multiple sampled generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further increasing model_calls); (iii) enable repair iterations and instrument repair_applied counters so repair coverage > 0 can be observed; (iv) increase device fidelity (hardware or higher‑fidelity emulation) to reduce simulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk. Each modification produces directly verifiable changes in the execution manifest (model_calls_used, hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied flags) and therefore supports clear replication and auditability.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal validity: the shared_candidate design removes generator variance intentionally; this choice was preregistered and reduces internal variance but also makes the confirmatory estimand narrower. Construct validity: the deterministic acceptance metric operationalizes correctness per validator rules but does not capture human‑facing properties (explainability, maintainability). External validity: synthetic task corpus and Mininet‑derived emulation limit production generality; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) restrict multi‑model generality. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance (all pairs concordant) drives bootstrap CI to a point mass and yields p = 1.0 for McNemar; these are correct descriptors of the observed data but do not imply practical equivalence of architectures under independent operation.

Reproducibility notes and artifact locations. All artifacts supporting the execution, analysis, and claims are archived in the run bundle and referenced by the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). Key artifacts cited in this paper include the preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1; preregistration_sha256 recorded in the manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json. Per‑task validator traces (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) provide the canonical evidence for each scored decision and are suitable for automated verification of reported counts. The archival bundle and the manifest together allow deterministic recomputation of the paired_binary_analysis_v1 outputs using the preserved seeds and executor parameters.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted the identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run demonstrates how preregistered shared‑candidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity but, by design, do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, and concrete preregistered protocol modifications that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
